title: Price Sensitivity and Customer Willingness to Pay
description: Learn how price sensitivity works and how to measure and respond to customers' willingness to pay.

options.text: How much demand changes when price changes
How much it costs to produce a product
How competitors react to your pricing
How often customers compare prices online

interactions.teachingPreamble: Price sensitivity (also called price elasticity of demand) describes how much customer buying behavior changes in response to a price change. When Netflix raised its US plan price by $1 in 2019, most subscribers stayed — indicating low price sensitivity. When a gas station raises prices by $0.10, many drivers switch to the station across the street — indicating high price sensitivity.

interactions.prompt: A SaaS tool raised prices 10% and lost 2% of subscribers. A competing tool raised prices 5% and lost 15% of subscribers. What's the key insight?

options.text: The first tool has higher costs
The second tool's customers are far more price sensitive
Both tools should lower prices immediately
The second tool charges more overall

interactions.prompt: Which factor most reduces price sensitivity for a product?

options.text: Having many identical competitors in the market
The product being a large share of buyer's budget
High switching costs and few substitutes available
Transparent pricing published on comparison websites

interactions.teachingPreamble: Several factors determine how price sensitive customers are. Key drivers include: the availability of substitutes (more alternatives = more sensitivity), switching costs (high costs = less sensitivity), and the purchase's share of budget (bigger share = more sensitivity). Apple's ecosystem creates high switching costs — moving from iPhone to Android means losing iMessage, AirDrop, and app purchases — which keeps Apple's customers less price sensitive.

interactions.prompt: When customers perceive a product as unique with no close substitutes, their price sensitivity is ____ compared to commodity products.

options.text: Much higher
About the same
Much lower
Completely unpredictable

interactions.prompt: You run a B2B analytics platform. Enterprise clients love your product but your market research shows high price sensitivity among small businesses. You need to grow revenue. Do you:

options.text: Raise enterprise prices where sensitivity is low
Cut small business prices to drive volume
Keep one flat price for all segments
Offer a free plan to attract everyone

interactions.prompt: Which is a reliable method to measure willingness to pay before launching a product?

options.text: Asking customers 'would you buy this at $X?'
Van Westendorp survey with four price-related questions
Copying the market leader's price exactly
Setting the lowest possible price to guarantee sales

interactions.teachingPreamble: Willingness to pay (WTP) is the maximum price a customer will accept. Measuring it directly ('would you pay $50?') is unreliable because people overstate willingness in surveys. The Van Westendorp Price Sensitivity Meter asks four questions: at what price is it too expensive, too cheap, starting to get expensive, and a bargain? Slack used this type of research to find their $6.67-$12.50/user/month sweet spot before scaling their paid plans.

interactions.prompt: Rank these customer segments from LOWEST price sensitivity to HIGHEST price sensitivity: (a) Shoppers using a coupon app at a grocery store, (b) A hospital buying a life-saving medical device, (c) A startup choosing between identical cloud hosting providers, (d) A law firm buying specialized compliance software.

options.text: Coupon-using grocery shoppers
Hospital buying life-saving device
Startup comparing identical hosting providers
Law firm buying specialized compliance software

interactions.prompt: A new competitor just launched an almost identical product at 40% lower price. Your churn rate jumps from 3% to 11% monthly. What should you prioritize first?

options.text: Immediately match the competitor's lower price
Invest in differentiation features to reduce substitutability
Increase your marketing budget to outspend them
Ignore it and hope customers come back

interactions.priorContext: Previously you learned that low substitutability and high switching costs reduce price sensitivity. Now a near-identical competitor has entered your market, making your product highly substitutable and revealing that your customers were more price sensitive than expected.
